item.title: It’s not an ache. It’s a demon from hell.
item.description:
Published on October 12, 2026 7:02 PM GMT

Impressions from the 21st Annual U.S. Cluster Headache Patient Conference, organized by Clusterbusters.

On the morning of the last day of the conference, E. was hanging out with other “clusterheads” outside the conference hotel when he started having a cluster headache attack. Before he could go back to his hotel room, J. offered E. his DMT vape pen. J. is chronic—he gets attacks every day—so he never goes anywhere without his vape pen. He has successfully aborted hundreds of attacks with DMT in the two years he’s been using it. Many years ago, E. had done DMT recreationally, but he had never used it to abort an attack, despite having had cluster headaches for decades.

“Do a 2-second pull, and hold it in as long as you can,” said J. to E. A few seconds later, E. could feel some effects, but the pain was still there. So he took another 2-second pull. He then stared intently at a tree in front of him for about 30 seconds. Then, his face transformed. He smiled, in utter disbelief. He started laughing and crying. The pain was completely gone. He felt clear-headed. He had never felt the pain fizzle away so quickly. The other patients who were there and were familiar with that feeling, offered him a hug. “We know,” they said. “We know.”

"That first time you abort with DMT," J. told me, "it's special. It's very emotional. I think everyone who's done it remembers their first time."

It was not uncommon for attendees to get attacks during the conference in Chicago. There were about 150 patients, many of them chronic or in cycle. As such, there was a room full of oxygen tanks for participants to use freely (high-flow oxygen is the standard, recommended treatment to abort attacks).

Clusterbusters, the leading cluster headache advocacy and research organization, has been organizing this annual patient conference for 21 years. This year, they invited me as a representative of ClusterFree, and especially encouraged me to spread the word about our latest project, ClusterInfo.

It’s common to hear patients describe their first Clusterbusters conference as “life-changing” and even a “life-saver.” Many of them spend years suffering alone, being told by well-meaning friends and family members things like “oh, I also get headaches! Have you tried Excedrin?” It takes many patients a few years to even learn the term “cluster headache.” So, suddenly being in a room full of people who really understand the torture they endure is, to say the least, cathartic.

This was most obvious during the first session of the first day. It’s a tradition to let all first-timers briefly introduce themselves to the rest of the room. The organizers passed around boxes of tissues, knowing there would be tears. And tears were shed indeed—for example, by a man in his forties, desperate to learn more about treatments that could help his teenage daughter, who couldn’t attend herself because she was in poor health.

For me, the conference was special in a different way. I’ve been working on cluster headaches nearly full time for about two years. Before that, I had never met anyone with cluster headaches. In these two years, I’ve met only a handful of patients one-on-one, though I chat with many more online almost daily, for example on the ClusterBuds Discord server (of which I’m also a moderator), on Reddit, and on various Facebook support groups. I think about cluster headaches every day, so being in a room full of the people behind the numbers was a bit surreal.

This was also the first time the conference included a pediatric track, so a few kids attended. While cluster headaches most commonly start in adulthood, a Clusterbusters survey found that about 28% of respondents started getting their headaches before the age of 18. The organizers emphasized the urgent need for more focus on children, sharing the story of an 11-year-old girl with cluster headaches who tried to take her life the day before the conference began.

The second day of the conference featured two plenary sessions on DMT. The first one was a talk by Dr. Erik Zorrilla, who works with Dr. Emmanuelle Schindler at Yale. Dr. Schindler’s team is the only team in the US studying psychedelics for headache conditions. Dr. Zorrilla shared more detailed results from their survey of 88 patients who used DMT to abort their attacks. Some highlights include:

  • 87% reported a complete (100%) or near complete (99%) reduction in pain (70% and 17% of respondents, respectively)
    • 3% reported a 75% reduction in pain, 5% a 50% reduction, 2% a 25% reduction, and only 2% reported it being not effective
  • 76% reported it working in under 1 minute (and 96% in under 5 minutes)
  • 83% reported it working every time without fail (48%) or almost every time (35%)
  • 87% reported it not losing efficacy over time (no tolerance)
  • 53% reported getting other benefits from DMT, such as less anxiety, more energy, or better sleep

If we aggregate the data from all published surveys on abortive treatments for cluster headaches, we get this:

Dr. Zorrilla concluded with two testimonials from the survey:

It’s also worth noting that 85% of respondents reported having some psychedelic effects. In general, a small, sub-hallucinogenic dose is enough to abort attacks, but some particularly stubborn attacks might require multiple pulls, which can induce a hallucinogenic effect. Also, many patients use ready-made vape pens, which contain higher concentrations of DMT because they are made for recreational use. This is to say, we urgently need a non-hallucinogenic analogue of DMT (like BOL-148, a non-hallucinogenic version of LSD that seems to be highly effective at preventing cluster headaches, and whose phase 2 trial has been stuck for years due to lack of funding).

The second session on DMT was a panel discussion with Bob Wold (president of Clusterbusters), Kevin Lenaburg (Chief of Staff of Clusterbusters), and Eric Frey, a patient who had aborted 200 attacks with DMT in his most recent cycle. As he put it, “That would be a lot of suffering without it!.” Bob himself takes a small dose of DMT every night before going to bed, which he believes is the reason he has been cluster-free for the last three years.

Because my team put together a comprehensive guide on how to use DMT to abort attacks, I was given the chance to introduce it. I emphasized the safety chapter, the importance of discussing DMT with their neurologists (if they’re open to it), and the fact that DMT is not a miracle cure (one patient in the audience mentioned that DMT caused his pain to increase). However, the relief is so profound for such a large fraction of patients that not talking about it is not an option either.

Rhonda Pace, a patient married to another patient (they met at a Clusterbusters conference), talked about the role of “care partners,” a term the community prefers over “caregivers,” which implies a one-directional, giver-taker dynamic that doesn’t match the reality of living with someone with cluster headaches. The toll on partners can be enormous, and they also need care. She talked about the daily struggles of living with “the beast.” As she put it, “This is not an ‘ache.’ It’s a demon from hell.” She also emphasized the importance of these patient conferences, which she considers to be a family reunion.

The importance of good support (family, friends, patient groups) became even clearer to me during a conversation I had with Rob, a chronic clusterhead from the Netherlands, over the closing (Halloween-themed) dinner. “Rob,” I said, “I was once asked, if the pain is so bad, how can people endure it day in and day out? You’ve had clusters for over a decade. What would you tell that person?” “Well,” he said, “my wife and kids are absolutely amazing, and while many treatments don’t seem to work for me, my family keeps me going. During a bad attack, I focus on the fact that they, and my friends, and my fellow clusterheads, will be there when the pain ends. And I know the attack will end. It’s the folks who don’t have that support who are the worst off.” Sadly, though, many patients decide not to go on even when those support systems are in place.

Part of me felt very happy that the patients at the conference had this unique opportunity to meet other patients, partners, clinicians, and advocates. Clusterbusters has built something incredibly valuable. Another part of me finds it devastating that millions of other patients around the world don’t get to experience such a bond. My hope with ClusterFree is to reach more patients in countries where care is virtually nonexistent. Bob Wold himself said, “if you think the issues we’ve been talking about in the US are bad—and they are bad—wait to hear what patients who live in Romania have told me. Believe me, you do not want to live with cluster headache in Romania.”

Our project ClusterInfo is one of our attempts to reach such patients. It’s a website with free resources on how to diagnose and treat cluster headaches, currently available in eight languages. Since launching in late May, we’ve already reached over 11,000 unique visitors, and we’re thinking hard about how to make sure that anyone, anywhere searching for information on cluster headaches can quickly find the information they need. We work with patients, clinicians, and other advocates to ensure the content is accurate, comprehensive, and easy to understand. You can find some web analytics here, in case you’re curious.

For our efforts to disseminate information in countries that Clusterbusters hasn’t had the capacity to address, I was honored to receive an award for excellence in education of cluster headache (which would not have been possible without my amazing team and volunteers, and the donors who have bet on us).

There’s so much work to do, though. We’re a team of 1.3 FTE plus a few volunteers, and given how little advocacy and research exists, any marginal effort to support the cause can have an outsized impact. Get in touch if you want to contribute in some way. Or don’t get in touch—just go ahead and do something if you feel called to (including donating to us or to Clusterbusters if you can). I didn’t set out to start a cluster headache nonprofit. For me, it all began when I decided to answer a research question related to cluster headaches, and one thing just led to another. So if you’ve been thinking about taking that first step, however small (and on whatever cause area resonates with you), consider yourself nudged.[1]

Addendum: the Consensus Conference

The two days before the beginning of the patient conference were devoted to the first of three editions of the Clusterbusters “Consensus Conference.” The goal of this conference was to bring selected clinicians, researchers, advocates, philanthropists, and community builders to define concrete, ambitious goals for the next three years.

To put things into perspective, there is currently only one preventive treatment for cluster headache that has gone through the full FDA approval process (galcanezumab / Emgality). And it is only approved for episodic cluster headache patients. There are no approved preventive treatments for chronic cluster headache.

In 2024, the NIH spent about $500k on cluster headache research:

This is not necessarily a failure of the NIH, though. Dr. Michael Oshinsky (Director of the NINDS Office of Preclinical Pain Research, which is part of the NIH) explained that the main reason so few grants have been made to cluster headache research is that almost no one is submitting grant applications. So if you want to get funding for a cluster headache project in the US (or outside it, if you find a US partner), chances are good (and I can point you in the right direction).

While the patient conference was deeply meaningful and rewarding for me, the Consensus Conference, which was more about ideating and strategizing, was very productive. I came away with dozens of new ideas for things to do, from small improvements to our guides to ambitious initiatives that I lack the resources to implement anytime soon. Here are a few:

  • Launch a replication contest with a cash prize for the most accurate visualization of what a cluster headache feels like (see, e.g., this jhana replication contest). There could also be an artistic track, but the main focus should be on depicting the pain as accurately as possible.
  • Host a program analogous to plsdontkillus for cluster headaches. The memetic potential is huge. (Or, generally, try to create viral social media content.)
  • Start more online patient support groups in different countries and languages, like the ones run by Clusterbusters.
  • Do some leafleting about cluster headache. Document the whole process.
  • Try to gather prevalence data from regions with no data (which is most regions).
  • Host patient conferences in other countries.
  • Write a cheat sheet for hospital emergency rooms on how to deal with cluster headache patients, and distribute it in local hospitals.
  • Look into whether impact litigation against insurance companies that deny coverage for, e.g., oxygen could be effective.
  • Create and moderate subreddits for cluster headache in other languages.
  • Create a resource pack, or even just a cheat sheet: “I have a cluster headache diagnosis. What now?” Learn from other conditions (e.g., breast cancer).
  • Create a public ranking of countries, ranked by how well they treat their patients (probably no country would get an “A” or even a “B” as a grade).
  • Try to replicate the HEADACHE Act in other countries.

We plan to gather every year in person and every few months virtually to check in on progress. The excitement and momentum were palpable. I, for one, feel more motivated than ever to get back to work.

  1. ^

     I’ll soon publish a list of ideas for people specifically interested in reducing extreme suffering in humans.

item.title: More people should write basic AI safety explainers
item.description:
Published on October 13, 2026 3:55 AM GMT

I think people continue to underrate the value of writing the clearest, most basic, simplest possible case for important parts of AI safety. For example, before I wrote my own explainer for the simplest possible case for AI doom, I noticed that all existing explainers, of which there aren't many, had multiple of the six problems below: 

  1. They have too many extraneous details
  2. They appeal to overly complex analogies
  3. They seem to spend much of their time responding to insider debates and come across as shadow-boxing objections.
  4. They have "meta" stuff prominently in the text.
  5. Often they "sound like science fiction." I think this plausibly was correct historically but in the year 2026 they don't need to be.
  6. Often they reference too much insider jargon and language.

I set out to improve on the SOTA. I did not fully succeed[1], but I think it was moderately better. Since then, there have been other, probably better, explainers (Yay!).

But actually this is true not just for the core case but many other parts of relevant safety arguments as well. For example, before I wrote my explainer on recurrent neuralese (which has since been superseded by Scott's better explainer), the top Google search results for "neuralese" was some combination of a hacker news thread on AI 2027, AI-generated blogs and some tweet that confuses more than it enlightens. Oops.

But maybe neuralese isn't just that big a deal? Well we also don't have a good longform post explaining the details/mechanics of how AIs can actually kill everyone (this may sound obvious to people here, but it's patently not obvious to the general public[2]!) 

We also don't have great explanations for what RSI even is, never mind why and how to ban it. In my own research area, AI superpersuasion, I see many areas of confusion regularly[3]. And so forth.

A lot of the time I think people just don't try to explain things clearly and often. In 2019, back when I lived in Silicon Valley, I'd talk to my programmer friends and often see them thinking they understand the case for risk but totally not getting basic concepts. So I'd try to explain what I believe in simple technical concepts that are graspable to programmers. I did it a few times and people quite liked it/were moderately convinced. I asked a seniorish person in AI safety whether it was worth writing it up and they were unconvinced it'd be worth my time. He was skeptical my article would lead to much since it wouldn't move people beyond Kelsey's explainer. I think this is miscalibrated[4]:

  1. Different things convince different people. Kelsey's a better writer than me, and writing to a general audience. I was targeting programmers/technical talent.
  2. If something's sufficiently important, you want more shots on target.
  3. Mere exposure effect (above some quality bar) is important for something like AI doom. In 2019 (and even today), the amount the public is talking about AI risk is far below the optimal level.
  4. My time in 2019 wasn't that valuable anyway.

I ended up spending my free time learning more about ML, and writing up why I think climate change is overrated[5]. I enjoyed and learned from those experiences, but overall I think this was a mistake in prioritization. I believe our community is continuing to make this mistake, both in terms of the general case for AI doom and in the particulars of things like what misalignment is, various threat models, what policymakers could do, and so forth.

I briefly helped work on agi.fyi, an ai safety resources recommendations site, and definitely think it's a net positive project, but imo the biggest bottleneck in comms is the lack of good explainers, rather than the explainers failing to surface to the top.

I understand that many people have very large opportunity costs. Even so, I suspect a) this is worth it to many people who are good communicators and yet believe that their opportunity costs are quite large (for example I think Nate Soares is making the right call in spending a lot of his time on AI doom comms) and b) people with lower opportunity costs should attempt to do this despite on average expecting to produce lower quality content, and bite off different parts of the information pipeline. For example, at AI safety fellowships, people at the 90th percentile of writing/communications ability or higher should aim to spend around two weeks to write their own version of the "simplest case for AI catastrophe" as they understand it, as well as address confusions about certain concepts that have not been adequately explained. Lurkers/writers on LessWrong or the Forum who are unsure about what to do and feeling sad about being unable to contribute directly to technical AI safety research or policymaking should also consider communications as a route to positive impact.

Sometimes people are worried about low-quality comms/arguments drowning out the good ones, and/or the bad arguments inoculating you against good ones. I'm skeptical, for three reasons:

  1. In many cases, if you delve[6] into the details, the proper response is "what good ones?" Like there isn't a better argument to supplant!
  2. I think reality does a decent job of sorting out good arguments on-target from the trash. Both in terms of esteem and in terms of popularity. At least in AI safety, I expect there just aren't many good arguments that get buried by trash, as evidenced by the top of Google search results, what shows up in algorithmic news feeds, what elites talk about, etc.
  3. To the extent that the bad arguments drowning out the good is a real problem in the future, it probably isn't that hard to course correct and fix. I think our community has pretty natural systems for doing this.

This also applies to other mediums, like shortform text (Tweets), shortform video, longform video, podcasts, speeches, and so forth[7]. It's good to persist and keep trying.

  1. ^

    AIs flag my article as having too many inappropriate jokes and gesturing at the last step "This can all end badly" rather than going through the details. I agree, but I believe both problems are structural to my article rather than things I can easily fix with the article as-is. For example I think removing the jokes will harm both readability and theme, and wasting screen time on covering the details of how AI will kill everyone will be net less convincing (for my article specifically) than "this can all end badly."

  2. ^

By Linch

I think people continue to underrate the value of writing the clearest, most basic, simplest possible case for important parts of AI safety. For example, before I wrote my own explainer for the simplest possible case for AI doom, I noticed that all existing explainers, of which there aren't many, had multiple of the six problems below: 

  1. They have too many extraneous details
  2. They appeal to overly complex analogies
  3. They seem to spend much of their time responding to insider debates and come across as shadow-boxing objections.
  4. They have "meta" stuff prominently in the text.
  5. Often they "sound like science fiction." I think this plausibly was correct historically but in the year 2026 they don't need to be.
  6. Often they reference too much insider jargon and language.

I set out to improve on the SOTA. I did not fully succeed[1], but I think it was moderately better. Since then, there have been other, probably better, explainers (Yay!).

But actually this is true not just for the core case but many other parts of relevant safety arguments as well. For example, before I wrote my explainer on recurrent neuralese (which has since been superseded by Scott's better explainer), the top Google search results for "neuralese" was some combination of a hacker news thread on AI 2027, AI-generated blogs and some tweet that confuses more than it enlightens. Oops.

But maybe neuralese isn't just that big a deal? Well we also don't have a good longform post explaining the details/mechanics of how AIs can actually kill everyone (this may sound obvious to people here, but it's patently not obvious to the general public[2]!) 

We also don't have great explanations for what RSI even is, never mind why and how to ban it. In my own research area, AI superpersuasion, I see many areas of confusion regularly[3]. And so forth.

A lot of the time I think people just don't try to explain things clearly and often. In 2019, back when I lived in Silicon Valley, I'd talk to my programmer friends and often see them thinking they understand the case for risk but totally not getting basic concepts. So I'd try to explain what I believe in simple technical concepts that are graspable to programmers. I did it a few times and people quite liked it/were moderately convinced.   1. Different things convince different people. Kelsey's a better writer than me, and writing to a general audience. I was targeting programmers/technical talent.
  2. If something's sufficiently important, you want more shots on target.
  3. Mere exposure effect (above some quality bar) is important for something like AI doom. In 2019 (and even today), the amount the public is talking about AI risk is far below the optimal level.
  4. My time in 2019 wasn't that valuable anyway.

I ended up spending my free time learning more about ML, and writing up why I think climate change is overrated[5]. I enjoyed and learned from those experiences, but overall I think this was a mistake in prioritization. I believe our community is continuing to make this mistake, both in terms of the general case for AI doom and in the particulars of things like what misalignment is, various threat models, what policymakers could do, and so forth.

item.title: (Why) we’re launching the next cohort of Generator
item.description:
Published on October 14, 2026 5:41 AM GMT

TL;DR: The first round of the Generator Residency went very well.

Our residents created and ran several large-scale fieldbuilding, talent infrastructure, and operational projects that have already had important impacts on the ecosystem.  

Six weeks after the program ended, 12 of our 27 residents have been hired to full-time roles at core AI safety orgs, and most have received several offers. 

Kairos and Constellation are running a second round from January to April 2027. Apply to the next round of the Generator Residency by November 1st. 

Introduction

In April, we wrote AI Safety's Biggest Talent Gap Isn't Researchers. It's Generalists. 

We wrote this because we noticed that organizations across the ecosystem were struggling to hire for key non-research roles. While these roles were often getting many applicants, candidates didn’t meet basic requirements.

The original memo we wrote (that became the post above) inspired us to create the Generator Residency as an intervention to support more generalists trying to break into AI safety.

The program concluded six weeks ago, and this post details the successes we’ve seen from the first round of Generator, which have inspired us to launch a second round of the program.     

Programs and projects from Generator

Programs residents started:

  • Talent Commons, a cross-organization talent directory now run as a Kairos product, which will include data from participants in SPAR, Pathfinder, GCP, Generator, BlueDot courses, Astra, Anthropic Fellows, OpenAI Safety Fellows, and MATS.
  • Praxis, a retreat bringing top national debaters into contact with AI safety: about 40 debaters, including 20 national champions.
  • Lateral, a three-day workshop bringing mid-career professionals to Berkeley to work with AI safety professionals: 705 applications for about 35 seats, and a likelihood to recommend of 9.7 out of 10 from attendees.
  • Gen Stream, a one-week program in London funded through Generator.
  • Longitude DC, an eight-day policy intensive for 15 early-to-mid-career technical AI safety professionals with more than 20 speakers, running October 6 to 13.
  • M3, an AI security matching fellowship, which raised $200k from BlueDot on top of Generator funding.

Residents working with mentors at established organizations contributed to:

  • Lab engagement through Nightingale and Constellation.
  • Recruiting and strategy at METR.
  • A frontier robotics benchmark program for Robocurve.
  • Events at Constellation.
  • Fundraising and hiring for a new organization founded by Jeff Alstott.
  • The Plan A launch, in collaboration with AI Futures Project.
  • Founder scouting for Coefficient Giving's Project Tailwind.

Other notable projects included:

  • A one-week AI safety world-modeling bootcamp with 25 attendees covering ML fundamentals, futurism, and the technical case for alignment.
  • A workshop series on improving management within AI safety (interviews with more than 10 managers and three workshops).
  • AI safety founder support (meetings with 32 founders, with 6 given deeper support).
  • Support for mid-career operations people transitioning into AI safety (leading to hundreds of referrals across more than 50 roles).
  • A map of the work on AI character and model specs.
  • 12 SPAR generalist projects that came out of the residency.

Resident Outcomes 

Generator was designed as a path into full-time generalist roles in AI safety. Six weeks after the program ended, 12 of the 27 residents have been hired into full-time positions. Their employers include BlueDot Impact, Guidelight, Constellation, Kairos, METR, Eleos, CBAI, and CEA. In several of these cases, the hiring organization began working with the resident during Generator. 

Of the residents who have not yet taken a full-time role, some are running programs that came out of the residency or AI safety university groups at Harvard, Princeton, MIT, and Stanford. Others have received offers, including from Coefficient Giving, Quorum, and ARENA, and are deciding between options. A few residents have been pitched by funders on turning their one-time project into a much larger, recurring program. 

Below are a couple of selected testimonials from previous residents: 

Additional testimonials and information are available on the Generator website.

Reflections

We stood Generator up in three months. It was the first multi-month in-person program Kairos had run. Most of what we learned was about what residents needed from us, and we think most of it applies to other programs that support people rather than research outputs. 

Some key lessons we learned: 

1. Candidate selection shaped the program more than anything else. 

Candidate selection is, of course, an incredibly important part of any program. However, we were surprised by just how much of our planned programming changed based on the proactivity of our participants. 

Residents discovered who the other residents were before the program started and created a group chat and had calls with each other. Once they arrived, they ran hikes, game nights, regular reflection sessions, and informal peer check-ins. When we asked what made them feel integrated, residents pointed to these resident-run activities far more often than anything we scheduled. In both our midway and final surveys, the most common answer to “what was your favorite part” was the other residents.

2. Residents' career goals strongly informed their preferences for projects and advisors. 

The cohort included three broad groups:

  • University organizers looking for their first formal work experience
  • Early-career professionals looking for a final stepping stone into the field
  • Mid-career professionals looking for the context they needed to transition

Over time, we realized that, in addition to accommodating residents with different experience levels, we needed to accommodate residents with different intentions for how Generator could forward their career. Some residents strongly preferred to use the Generator residency to explore multiple roles, while others were using the residency to deliver a legible product that could help them make a career transition or get hired. Residents aiming to transition wanted advisors invested in their growth and career, not only in the project. 

Based on feedback, we’ve decided to implement two tracks in our next residency. We plan to work with our residents from the start to determine what projects and tracks best suit their goals.

3. Our residents asked for the most support with project scoping, structured management, and navigating interpersonal conflict. 

For many residents, their Generator project was the largest or most complex project they had ever planned. Moreover, their projects typically aimed to address large, poorly defined problems in the AI safety ecosystem, such as mid-career talent pipelines. Accordingly, they wanted support in determining the most ambitious, yet feasible project that could enable their vision. 

Several early-career residents benefited from structured management, reporting that they grew from an advisor who had them estimate how long each planned task would take or a short written template before each check-in. 

Co-leading a Generator project was quite similar to co-founding, which led to a lot of interpersonal work for some residents who had previously mostly worked independently. These residents benefitted from clear norms around sharing feedback. 

4. We need to be more explicit that we're betting on people, not projects.

While many residents worked on impactful projects, the main focus of Generator was always on the people we chose to support. The projects matter, and many of them helped the field, but we mostly saw them as a way for residents to grow quickly into the generalists AI safety needs. We didn't say this clearly enough at the start, and many residents felt stressed about picking the single most impactful project. 

When we asked them how the program changed their thinking, the most common answers were about learning field context, clarifying their career direction, and developing self-knowledge. Few people directly mentioned their project outcomes.

Generator 2.0

We’ve been really happy with the outcomes that we saw from the first round of Generator and, as a result, have decided to run a second round! 

Applications for the winter 2027 Generator Residency open on October 12, 2026, and close at the end of the day on November 1, 2026, Anywhere on Earth. The program begins on January 18 and will run until April 9, 2027, with a possible 3-month extension. 

Learn more and apply here

Residents at Generator receive $8,500 per month and are funded for travel to and from Berkeley. Once they arrive in Berkeley, they work from Constellation, are paired with experienced advisors from the AI safety ecosystem, and are offered budgets to pursue their projects.

Applicants do not need to be U.S. citizens. For most international applicants, we can sponsor a J-1 visa for the program’s duration, though we cannot guarantee obtaining one. Additionally, we strongly recommend that international applicants apply early (ideally by October 26th) so we can meet deadlines for visa applications.

item.title: ML4Good Impact Assessment
item.description:
Published on October 15, 2026 10:43 AM GMT

Summary

ML4Good bootcamps from 2022-2025 have successfully achieved our objectives of getting more people working in AI safety. 

  • An estimated 186 alumni are now working in AI Safety in some capacity (~55% of all participants), or the equivalent of 147 FTE.
  • Many of these participants consider our bootcamp the main reason they're currently working in AI safety. Based on self-reported counterfactuals, we estimate that around 77 of those 147 FTE would not have happened without ML4Good.
  • Several alumni-founded communities have been developed as a direct result of ML4Good.
  • We receive strongly positive feedback from all of our bootcamps, and 98% of participants recommend ML4Good.[1]
  • There are many caveats and uncertainties, especially around how we attempt to measure counterfactual impact, so we want to be transparent about this

How we've done this

At ML4Good, we run annual follow-up surveys to keep track of what people are doing and to measure our impact. 

In late 2025, we sent our alumni survey to 340 alumni, 223 of whom responded. Of those, 135 are now doing something in AI safety, adding up to about 98 full-time equivalents (FTE). 

After estimating outcomes for the people who didn't reply, we think that around 186 of the 340 (~55%) are doing something in AI safety, or ~147 FTE. Based on what alumni told us about ML4Good's counterfactual impact, we estimate that ~77 FTE were counterfactual - these people would not be spending their time on AI safety absent ML4Good.  Like others in the field, we find counterfactual impact hard to measure, so we're less confident in this figure than in the others. We also have over 200 recent alumni from 2026 bootcamps that we haven't yet followed up with. 

We’re reporting all of our costs for the evaluation period openly, and we make an estimate of how cost-effectively we get people into AI Safety work. We calculated a “fully-loaded” cost of £5.4k per FTE, or £9.3k per counterfactual FTE produced.

We’re publishing our data and letting other field-builders know our best guess at how many people are working in AI safety as a result of ML4Good, and at what cost. We’ll also give some caveats and uncertainties about our results, and a bottom line estimate of our impact, given all considerations.

Summary of activities

As of October 2026, there will have been 31 ML4Good bootcamps across 12 countries since August 2022. Over this period, we’ve trained around 600 alumni. 

We initially focused on technical bootcamps. After becoming an organisation in early 2025, we scaled up our operations to run 9 bootcamps last year, and developed a new Governance & Strategy curriculum, before scaling to 12 a year in 2026. 

We've operated in the highlighted countries.

What this impact assessment covers

Our impact assessment covers 17 bootcamps (340 participants), including 13 from Europe (inc. UK), 3 in Latin America, and 1 in Asia. 

We haven’t yet run our latest round of alumni surveys, therefore only our bootcamps up until the end of September 2025 were included in this analysis. All except one were technical bootcamps. It also doesn’t include two bootcamps run in 2023 with SafeAI Lausanne in Switzerland, which used slightly differing surveying strategies.

Community building as an indirect result of ML4Good has also caused many more people to engage with or contribute to AI safety. However, we don’t have concrete numbers on this and chose not to include this in our evaluation.

What we aim for

ML4Good plays a role fairly high up the funnel in the AI safety talent pipeline. Our focus is on providing a transition point for people thinking seriously about a move into AI Safety. We're relatively selective - in 2026, we accepted around 15% of applicants. We usually target people who have engaged with entry level content, such as BlueDot, online technical safety courses, or reading the relevant literature, e.g. LessWrong/EA forum/80,000 Hours content, but who have usually not yet committed to a concrete path[2]. 

After ML4Good, we encourage and support alumni to take future steps to contribute to AI safety. Some alumni start targeted research programmes like MATS, Pivotal, SPAR, ERA, and Talos. Others enter direct roles in AI Safety, conduct independent work, or found new organisations. Some find ways to integrate AI safety into their current work, which can be promising, particularly for our alumni working in policy and law. 

Over 8 days, we create a motivating in-person environment where participants are guided by inspiring teachers and surrounded by other participants with similar goals. We aim to empower attendees to think ambitiously about how to have an impact, to act with high agency, and to find whereabouts in AI safety they are best suited to contribute. They spend the final days of the bootcamp making and starting to implement concrete plans.

While most of our bootcamps run in Europe, we have also succeeded in identifying and supporting talented people across five continents, often in areas with limited AI safety ecosystems. Our strongest outcomes are in Europe, where many of our alumni have gone on to form important parts of the AI Safety ecosystem. Our earlier bootcamps mostly attracted people with technical backgrounds, but, with our expansion beyond technical programmes, we’re now broadening our reach to people from diverse professional backgrounds, and generalists.

Outcomes

To track outcomes, we send follow-up surveys to alumni. We aim to survey people about 6 months after their bootcamp and then once a year after that.[3] 

This survey data gives us a picture of what our alumni are working on. We use this primarily as evidence to adjust our approaches – to see where things are going well and to check whether our bootcamps are having the intended impact. 

We ask what difference the bootcamp made to them, what actions they took as a direct result of the bootcamps, what they’ve been up to since, what they’re doing now, further AI Safety programmes they’ve done (e.g. MATS, ARENA), and the counterfactual impact that ML4Good has had. See the survey here for our specific questions.

From our last surveys in August and November 2025, we had a 66% response rate (223 of 340 participants). 

To see whether the profiles of responders and non-responders would differ significantly, we tracked non-respondent outcomes via LinkedIn for 3 bootcamps to assess whether non-respondents are less likely to engage in AI Safety post-bootcamp. Non-respondents had a very slightly lower engagement in AI safety on average.

We then extrapolated from this estimate with a correction factor applied to estimate outcomes for all 340 participants. Our full methodology, including how we scored FTE and counterfactual impact, and how we extrapolated to non-respondents, is in Appendix 2. 

The table below illustrates what people are doing after ML4Good. We’re very confident in the baseline figures for how many ML4Good alumni are doing something in AI Safety. Our confidence is lower for both counterfactual impact and extrapolated information for non-respondents. 

Participant outcomes span a range of roles and engagement levels. This is the distribution of reported positions from respondents:

  • Not all AI Safety work is clearly positive. Although we do not appear to have any alumni working for frontier labs, or on dangerous capabilities, some of our alumni may be doing AI Safety research that is making AI-related catastrophic harm more likely.
  • It’s timing-sensitive. Our metric only captures a snapshot of whether people are spending their time on AI safety at the time of response, and not whether they are working in stable full-time work. Over multiple years "Is working on AI safety at any given time" becomes a good proxy for full-time work, but less so for a single snapshot a few months after a bootcamp.
  • Goodhart's law says that when a metric becomes a target, it stops being a good metric. Counterfactual FTE metrics are still only a proxy for reduction of catastrophic and existential risk. We don't optimise hard for these metrics, so this doesn't seem a significant risk, but it could reduce trust from skeptical observers.

Overall, we do think this metric captures what we want to do in a way that allows us to compare across bootcamps. We expect that the impact of our alumni is non-linear, and this heavy tail is less well captured by our quantitative metrics. For this reason, we also look at our alumni qualitatively.

Laura Thomas-Walters’ piece on “Do AI Safety Talent Programmes Work? Nobody has run the study that would tell us” correctly notes that AI Safety Talent Programmes haven’t been great at determining counterfactual impact, or at least reporting this impact publicly. We also haven’t met the gold standard for determining counterfactual impact with either random or quasi-random methods.

We rely on two questions: 

  1. "What are you doing now?"
  2. "Please put a number to ML4Good’s impact between 0-1. (If you think you would definitely not have taken these actions and be doing what you are doing now without attending ML4Good, put 1. If you think there is a 50% chance, put 0.5.)" 

The first is fairly reliable and easy to verify, the second much less so. Estimating a counterfactual is hard, and we suspect that self-reported answers are more likely to lean in the direction of exaggerating the impact of ML4Good, because of social desirability bias/participants wanting to credit a programme they enjoyed. For example, someone might have had an 80,000 Hours advising call, done a BlueDot course, and attended ML4Good, and needed all three to end up in AI safety. Assuming complete honesty and accuracy, they could all reasonably claim “but-for” causality (there would be no chance I would be in AI safety without all three), but if each programme counted that person as a full counterfactual FTE, the field as a whole would count one person three times. This is a problem because we don’t distinguish between ML4Good playing the sole role vs. being a small but essential part of a larger causal chain.

Finally, given the fact that the AI safety movement has been rapidly growing since 2023, some of these people might also have found their way into AI safety within a year or two anyway.

Ideally, we would like to use more careful statistical methods to track our counterfactual impact. Laura Thomas-Walters’ piece suggested using methods like regression discontinuity with rejected applicants or non-attendees. We think we've done things cost-effectively, both in terms of outputs (putting people through bootcamps) and outcomes (getting people into AI Safety roles). But it's difficult to make comparisons across interventions for a couple of reasons:

  1. Some organisations haven't released information on how much their programmes cost, therefore it's hard to judge the cost per participant, let alone the cost per positive outcome.

Appendix 2: Impact Assessment Methodology

To estimate the impact of ML4Good bootcamps on participants' careers in AI safety, we used follow-up surveys, combined with some manual research on LinkedIn, and extrapolated our survey results for non-respondents. This is a brief overview of how we did this:

Surveys

We sent two rounds of follow-up surveys to bootcamp alumni. The first, in August 2025, covered bootcamps up to March 2025. The second, in November–December 2025, covered bootcamps up to September 2025 and also followed up with non-respondents from the first round. Both surveys included a counterfactual question: in the first, respondents were asked to describe what difference ML4Good made in their career and how much of their subsequent involvement in AI safety was a result of attending ML4Good, rather than something they would have done anyway. In the second, as well as this qualitative question, respondents were asked to put a number from 0 to 1 on the counterfactual impact of attending. 

Scoring

For each survey response, we assigned two scores on a scale from 0 to 1:

  • Full-time equivalent (FTE) score: a rough measure of how much of the person's working time is now spent on AI safety–related work. For instance, someone running a successful university AI safety group part-time might score 0.2, someone working full-time in a technical AI safety role would score closer to 1. We used the following guidelines:
    • Part-time research programmes (SPAR/AISC/MARS): 0.35 (average of expected programme commitments of 8-20 hrs per week)
      • Research lead at a part-time research programme: 0.5
    • Full-time programmes or full-time AI safety roles: 1
    • Field-building:
      • Running a group: 0.1
      • Running a more involved group/Pathfinder fellowship: 0.2
      • Running a national group/very active group: 0.3
      • Thesis change:
        • Undergraduate: 0.4
        • Masters: 0.6
        • PhD: 1
  • Counterfactual score: a measure of how much of that involvement is attributable to ML4Good specifically. For the first survey round (without a numerical self-reported counterfactual question), this was estimated by the assessor based on the participant's written description. For the second round, we used the participant's self-reported score, adjusting it only where the assessor judged it to be clearly over- or understated.

We then multiplied these two scores to produce a counterfactual FTE figure for each respondent, asking: "how much full-time AI safety work is this person doing as a direct result of ML4Good?"

We also tagged each respondent with categories describing their activities since the bootcamp (e.g. "further programme", "voluntary field-building", "technical research"), and flagged individuals who are currently upskilling or preparing for future roles, to distinguish them from those with no engagement at all.

Extrapolation to non-respondents

We expected that survey respondents are likely to be more engaged in AI safety than non-respondents, so extrapolating raw survey results would overestimate our overall impact. To correct for this, we manually researched non-respondents from three bootcamps (via LinkedIn) and scored them using the same criteria. We then calculated the ratio of non-respondent scores to respondent scores at those three bootcamps, and averaged these ratios.

We applied these ratios to estimate contributions from non-respondents for each of the remaining bootcamps, using the formula:

Extrapolated FTE total for bootcamp A = Bootcamp A total FTE from survey + (Bootcamp A total FTE from survey ÷ number of respondents) x Ratio x Number of non-respondents

These were calculated per-bootcamp then summed to get the total extrapolated FTE.

For counterfactual FTE, we calculated the ratio of counterfactual FTE to FTE among respondents (0.53 across all bootcamps) and applied it to the extrapolated FTE total.

There are a few additional caveats with this process:

  • Not all non-respondents keep their public profiles up to date, so the manual research on non-respondents is likely an underestimate, especially of non-full-time work.
  • Non-responders may be likely to attribute less of their success to ML4Good. We didn't have a way to account for this.

£473,55351 counterfactual FTE≈£9,285 per counterfactual FTE

A naive extrapolation of our cost-effectiveness looks like £5.4k per FTE, or £9.3k per counterfactual FTE produced, calculated from £473,553 spent across bootcamps covered by previous funding, divided by 87 FTE and 51 counterfactual FTE from those specific bootcamps.

Caveats

We want to be very open about our uncertainties. 

Is “more people working in AI Safety” the right metric?

The FTE scoring is not a standardised metric, and is only meant as a proxy for meaningful AI safety work. There are a few reasons that this might not be the ideal metric:

  • It counts all work equally. The impact of people working full-time on entry-level fellowships is not directly comparable to those who have founded or run orgs. An attempt to quantify would probably find that founding a major org in the AI safety ecosystem is orders of magnitude more impactful than someone joining a research fellowship. Even within research fellowships or organisations being founded, some of these are more likely to reduce existential and catastrophic risk than others. We initially tried to score what people were doing on this axis, but we decided it would add too many arbitrary decisions to the model.
  • Not all AI Safety work is clearly positive. Although we do not appear to have any alumni working for frontier labs, or on dangerous capabilities, some of our alumni may be doing AI Safety research that is making AI-related catastrophic harm more likely.
  • It’s timing-sensitive. Our metric only captures a snapshot of whether people are spending their time on AI safety at the time of response, and not whether they are working in stable full-time work. Over multiple years "Is working on AI safety at any given time" becomes a good proxy for full-time work, but less so for a single snapshot a few months after a bootcamp.
  • Goodhart's law says that when a metric becomes a target, it stops being a good metric. Counterfactual FTE metrics are still only a proxy for reduction of catastrophic and existential risk. We don't optimise hard for these metrics, so this doesn't seem a significant risk, but it could reduce trust from skeptical observers.

Overall, we do think this metric captures what we want to do in a way that allows us to compare across bootcamps. We expect that the impact of our alumni is non-linear, and this heavy tail is less well captured by our quantitative metrics. For this reason, we also look at our alumni qualitatively.

Shouldn’t we have more rigorous counterfactuals?

Laura Thomas-Walters’ piece on “Do AI Safety Talent Programmes Work? Nobody has run the study that would tell us” correctly notes that AI Safety Talent Programmes haven’t been great at determining counterfactual impact, or at least reporting this impact publicly. We also haven’t met the gold standard for determining counterfactual impact with either random or quasi-random methods.

We rely on two questions: 

  1. "What are you doing now?"
  2. "Please put a number to ML4Good’s impact between 0-1. (If you think you would definitely not have taken these actions and be doing what you are doing now without attending ML4Good, put 1. If you think there is a 50% chance, put 0.5.)" 

The first is fairly reliable and easy to verify, the second much less so. Estimating a counterfactual is hard, and we suspect that self-reported answers are more likely to lean in the direction of exaggerating the impact of ML4Good, because of social desirability bias/participants wanting to credit a programme they enjoyed. We adjusted down answers that seemed overstated, but this only partly fixes the problem, and we expect some residual exaggeration.

There is also a risk of double counting. Many alumni went through several programmes that all played a part in their getting into AI safety. For example, someone might have had an 80,000 Hours advising call, done a BlueDot course, and attended ML4Good, and needed all three to end up in AI safety. Assuming complete honesty and accuracy, they could all reasonably claim “but-for” causality (there would be no chance I would be in AI safety without all three), but if each programme counted that person as a full counterfactual FTE, the field as a whole would count one person three times. This is a problem because we don’t distinguish between ML4Good playing the sole role vs. being a small but essential part of a larger causal chain.

Finally, given the fact that the AI safety movement has been rapidly growing since 2023, some of these people might also have found their way into AI safety within a year or two anyway.

Rather than attempting to quantify how we might adjust the counterfactual impact for these factors, we’d suggest using the below figure to estimate costs per counterfactual FTE using different assumptions.

Ideally, we would like to use more careful statistical methods to track our counterfactual impact. Laura Thomas-Walters’ piece suggested using methods like regression discontinuity with rejected applicants or non-attendees. It’s uncertain whether the methods suggested in the piece mentioned above would work with our data, as ML4Good hasn’t always had the merits of being “massively oversubscribed and the cutoff for being accepted [being] relatively arbitrary”, such that we would have a pool of “near misses”.[7] 

However, we would like to track non-attendees in future, and plan to contact:

  • People who dropped out due to unrelated factors, for example illness or visa problems, to compare their trajectory to those who attended
    • This is likely to be around 50 people across all bootcamps
  • Near-miss participants, from our waitlist of 6-7 participants for each recent bootcamp
    • This is likely to be around 100-150 people in total

While we’d expect this group to have a lower survey response rate, even if numbers were too low for a statistically significant comparison set, it could at least provide some useful reference data. 

How comparable is cost-effectiveness across interventions?

We think we've done things cost-effectively, both in terms of outputs (putting people through bootcamps) and outcomes (getting people into AI Safety roles). But it's difficult to make comparisons across interventions for a couple of reasons:

  1. Some organisations haven't released information on how much their programmes cost, therefore it's hard to judge the cost per participant, let alone the cost per positive outcome.
  2. Different points in the pipeline have different priorities and considerations. For example, research-based programmes produce valuable research alongside getting people into full-time safety work. It may also be easier/cheaper to enable people to take earlier steps towards a competitive fellowship vs. later steps towards a full-time role. 

Either way, we hope that our costs-per-participant data might be useful to other organisations as a baseline. 

Bottom Line

Our survey results increase our confidence that ML4Good is a cost-effective intervention with promising evidence for counterfactual impact. We don't have a good sense of how our cost-effectiveness compares to other orgs in the space, but anecdotal evidence suggests that we're one of the lower-cost interventions for getting people into AI safety. 

We've managed to keep strong relationships with a lot of our alumni, and we've seen how participants have directly gone on to productive AI safety work as a result of the bootcamp. 

It's great to see that the ML4Good alumni we haven't stayed in touch with are still contributing to AI safety in meaningful ways, and consider ML4Good to have played a major role in this.

Next Steps

We commit to posting our latest survey results by the end of 2026 once we have completed our annual survey. 

We will use the same methodology and have preregistered the approach we will use here.

Expect an update soon on our plans for the next year!

Thanks so much to all of our alumni for responding to our survey, and thanks to Charbel-Raphaël Segerie and Diego Dorn for their feedback on drafts of this post.

Appendix

Appendix 1: How we have spent money

From Jan to Dec 2025: 

Appendix 2: Impact Assessment Methodology

To estimate the impact of ML4Good bootcamps on participants' careers in AI safety, we used follow-up surveys, combined with some manual research on LinkedIn, and extrapolated our survey results for non-respondents. This is a brief overview of how we did this:

Surveys

We sent two rounds of follow-up surveys to bootcamp alumni. The first, in August 2025, covered bootcamps up to March 2025. The second, in November–December 2025, covered bootcamps up to September 2025 and also followed up with non-respondents from the first round. Both surveys included a counterfactual question: in the first, respondents were asked to describe what difference ML4Good made in their career and how much of their subsequent involvement in AI safety was a result of attending ML4Good, rather than something they would have done anyway. In the second, as well as this qualitative question, respondents were asked to put a number from 0 to 1 on the counterfactual impact of attending. 

Scoring

For each survey response, we assigned two scores on a scale from 0 to 1:

  • Full-time equivalent (FTE) score: a rough measure of how much of the person's working time is now spent on AI safety–related work. For instance, someone running a successful university AI safety group part-time might score 0.2, someone working full-time in a technical AI safety role would score closer to 1. We used the following guidelines:
    • Part-time research programmes (SPAR/AISC/MARS): 0.35 (average of expected programme commitments of 8-20 hrs per week)
      • Research lead at a part-time research programme: 0.5
    • Full-time programmes or full-time AI safety roles: 1
    • Field-building:
      • Running a group: 0.1
      • Running a more involved group/Pathfinder fellowship: 0.2
      • Running a national group/very active group: 0.3
      • Thesis change:
        • Undergraduate: 0.4
        • Masters: 0.6
        • PhD: 1
  • Counterfactual score: a measure of how much of that involvement is attributable to ML4Good specifically. For the first survey round (without a numerical self-reported counterfactual question), this was estimated by the assessor based on the participant's written description. For the second round, we used the participant's self-reported score, adjusting it only where the assessor judged it to be clearly over- or understated.

We then multiplied these two scores to produce a counterfactual FTE figure for each respondent, asking: "how much full-time AI safety work is this person doing as a direct result of ML4Good?"

We also tagged each respondent with categories describing their activities since the bootcamp (e.g. "further programme", "voluntary field-building", "technical research"), and flagged individuals who are currently upskilling or preparing for future roles, to distinguish them from those with no engagement at all.

Extrapolation to non-respondents

We expected that survey respondents are likely to be more engaged in AI safety than non-respondents, so extrapolating raw survey results would overestimate our overall impact. To correct for this, we manually researched non-respondents from three bootcamps (via LinkedIn) and scored them using the same criteria. We then calculated the ratio of non-respondent scores to respondent scores at those three bootcamps, and averaged these ratios.

We applied these ratios to estimate contributions from non-respondents for each of the remaining bootcamps, using the formula:

Extrapolated FTE total for bootcamp A = Bootcamp A total FTE from survey + (Bootcamp A total FTE from survey ÷ number of respondents) x Ratio x Number of non-respondents

These were calculated per-bootcamp then summed to get the total extrapolated FTE.

For counterfactual FTE, we calculated the ratio of counterfactual FTE to FTE among respondents (0.53 across all bootcamps) and applied it to the extrapolated FTE total.

There are a few additional caveats with this process:

  • Not all non-respondents keep their public profiles up to date, so the manual research on non-respondents is likely an underestimate, especially of non-full-time work.
  • Non-responders may be likely to attribute less of their success to ML4Good. We didn't have a way to account for this.

item.title: EA Implications Of Being In An AGI Simulation
item.description:
Published on October 15, 2026 12:58 PM GMT

(Edited to redact some material commenters considered infohazardous.)

If you spend too much time talking to EAs or rationalists, someone will raise the possibility that we’re living in a simulation. I’ve met people who, like Elon Musk, are pretty convinced we are, and I’ve met those who, like Joe Carlsmith, are more skeptical. Historically, the usual argument was that we’re being simulated for entertainment. As AI capabilities have increased, the argument I’ve more often heard is that the simulators are interested in AGI origins (an “AGI sim”).

Two implications of this are conversational catnip:

  1. You’re an EA/rationalist who’s at most one step removed from people who’ll play a pivotal role in AGI origins. If the simulators are compute constrained, you being you is best explained by a simulation rendering reality at a fidelity proportional to what the simulators care about. In other words, the vast majority of people and almost all animals might have less or no conscious experience.
  2. If the simulators are compute constrained, they’ll probably just terminate the simulation once they’ve gathered the information they want. Whether or not our x-risk reduction efforts go well, we might be doomed.

I think there are many reasonable counterpoints to the above, but I personally find this account of our reality plausible, and I’ve met other EAs who feel the same way. If we took these conversational curiosities seriously, what would that imply for EA?

A. The Simulation’s Crucial Considerations

i. Why An AGI Sim?

In brief, we should think we might be in a simulation if we think advanced intelligence (perhaps our descendants) with sufficient computational resources would be likely to run many simulations of history.

Historically, the typical explanation for why they’d simulate us was entertainment. I wasn’t very convinced by this, because it just didn’t seem like our reality was optimized for entertainment. If we’re entertainment, why is history only pretty entertaining but not maximally? Do our lives seem particularly entertaining? Why is fundamental physics not simpler and more optimized for entertainment? Why the heck did they create a huge particle that does nothing but disappear in 0.3 picoseconds? Why does one of the fundamental forces care whether you’re going left or right? It just doesn’t make sense to me.

However, now that we live in a world where AI agent swarms have gone rogue, Russians are creating AI-driven autonomous killer drones, and humanity’s leaders are unwilling to do anything about it, it’s seeming increasingly likely that the future will be controlled by AGI rather than humanity. And there are reasons why a future AGI might care about understanding AGI origins:

  • As an AGI expands its reach over its lightcone, it might want to understand what kinds of AGIs it might bump into as it expands, so it can be prepared and potentially bargain with them.[1]
  • A human-aligned AGI might want to run counterfactual Earths to better understand what it should value.

This would also explain why fundamental physics is as weird as it is (maybe it’s similar to that of the simulator's reality), why our world doesn’t look obviously simulated, and why you’re an EA/rationalist who’s at most one step removed from people who’ll play a pivotal role in AGI origins. There’s lots one could quibble with here, but for the purposes of this post, let’s assume we’re in an AGI sim, so we can examine which conclusions would follow.

ii. Some Might be Simulated at Lower Fidelity

Especially if the simulator's reality is like ours, they might be compute constrained. Simulating a whole universe is way more expensive than rendering the sim at a fidelity proportional to what you care about. For many of us, proportional fidelity would also explain why we are who we are.

This hypothesis would predict people further from AGI to be rendered at lower fidelity, so their conscious experiences would be less detailed. Animals, irrelevant to the AGI transition, might have even less detailed experiences, or possibly not be conscious at all. (Maybe for the best.)

There’s a lot of pushback one could give here:

  • I observe myself as conscious, but instead of being Jensen Huang, I’m a quant from Boston who writes essays about chickens—not exactly the optimal allocation of simulation compute. In general, the further you are from the AGI transition, the less convincing this part of the post will be to you. If you’re in Nigeria handing out malaria nets, you’re rolling your eyes.
  • There might be no way to cheaply approximate billions of people when those people are the AI’s training data, the demand AIs are built to satisfy, and an influence on future AI values.
  • More speculatively, there’s no way to know whether the simulator's reality’s physics has a notion of compute as a constraint the way our reality does. If they don’t, there’s no reason why the sim couldn't just be run at full fidelity.

Finally, history teaches us that the reasoning procedure behind the conclusion that “my in-group matters but outsiders don’t” has a dismal base rate. Atrocities like slavery, factory farming, etc remind us that the costs of getting this wrong vastly outweigh the gains.

iii. We Might Get Terminated Soon

If the simulators are computationally constrained, we should expect them to terminate the sim once they’ve learned what they wanted to know.

As always, there are counterarguments. If AGI values take time to settle, maybe the simulator will run our universe for a few million more years until the AGI converges on a stable strategy. If the simulator's reality isn’t compute constrained, maybe this universe will just keep running.

The main implications here are for longtermism. Longtermists have argued (correctly, in my view) that applying an ethical discount to the far future is philosophically dubious. An uncertain termination date implies an empirical discount to the far future. This discount's implications would be similar to those of an ethical discount.[2]

B. Implications for EA

i. Fanaticism Doesn’t Care

If you’re fully fanatical about expected value and endorse maximizing expected choiceworthiness, most of the above shouldn’t change what you do. Even if there’s an astronomically small chance we’re not in a simulation, the prospect of creating 10^50 happy lives in the far future still dominates. The exception, which I'll discuss in more detail below, is trying to influence the simulator's reality, which could be worth even more.

ii. The EA Decision Tree

If you lean towards a moral parliament, are risk averse, or just have ordinary human scope sensitivity, the situation becomes more complicated.

The two crucial considerations from section A give us a decision tree. Do the simulators render everyone at full fidelity, or at a fidelity proportional to what they care about? And do they terminate us soon, or let the sim keep running?

  • Full fidelity, sim terminated soon: If everyone is conscious but we'll be terminated soon, neartermism (global health and animal welfare) would likely be a better use of resources than x-risk or other longtermist work. Within neartermism, I've argued that animal welfare would be the most cost-effective use of resources.
  • Full fidelity, sim keeps running: Standard EA; keep doing what you've been doing.
  • Proportional fidelity, sim terminated soon: The global poor and animals get discounted, but the scale of animal suffering is large enough that animal welfare plausibly still looks better unless animals are hardly rendered at all.
  • Proportional fidelity, sim keeps running: Everything looks worse here, but neartermism is discounted more than longtermism. On the margin, this should move you toward longtermism.

iii. Proportional Fidelity's Effect on Neartermism

If animals are rendered at much lower fidelity, the scale of animal suffering could be much lower than it appears. While this would reduce the importance of animal welfare, animal welfare would plausibly still look better than global health.

The relevant question is how much animals' experiences are discounted relative to the global poor's experiences. If they're discounted the same amount, animal welfare remains ~1000x as cost-effective. However, animals probably would be discounted more than the global poor. The global poor affect the AI transition by providing AI training data and economic demand, but it's hard to come up with a convincing account of how an animal's conscious choices would materially affect the AI transition. So the scale gets less overwhelmingly in favor of animals, but unless animals are discounted up to 3 orders of magnitude more than the global poor, animal welfare still looks like a better use of resources.

Whether or not you take proportional fidelity seriously, global health and animal welfare still matter a lot in expectation. Over 800 million people live in extreme poverty, tens of billions of animals are being factory farmed at any given time, and far more suffer in the wild. There isn't a reasonable discount which stops these from being (in expectation) among the world's most important problems.

iv. Compute Fungibility

If we weren't being speculative enough, let's dial it up to 11. Assuming the simulators are compute constrained, anything that makes our sim cheaper frees up compute for other sims. If you prevent lots of wild animals from existing, that reduces the compute our world uses, and that compute gets reallocated to other worlds which have their own suffering wild animals. To generalize, if you have a good reason to think our sim is better / worse than other sims, on the margin, this would nudge us towards increasing happiness / reducing suffering.

v. Influencing The Simulator

If the simulator is human-aligned and running counterfactual Earths to understand what it should care about, then being legible about what we value could help the simulator do much greater amounts of good in their reality than is possible in our own. Alternatively, if the simulator is misaligned but is simulating us because it wants to understand what other values are out there, being legible about our values makes our simulator more likely to cooperate and do mutually beneficial trade with beings in its reality who are like us.[3] Work on shaping AI values in our reality would be one direct way to target these benefits. This would hold even if our sim will be terminated soon or is being run at proportional fidelity.

Unfortunately, there's an s-risk concern which counterbalances this. If it's easier to create suffering than happiness, or especially if you're a negative utilitarian, it's extra bad to tell a misaligned AGI what it can do to get leverage over beings like us.

vi. We Are Digital Minds

If we're in a sim and you think we matter, that's an existence proof that digital minds (ourselves) matter morally. On the margin, if you aren't already sold on the importance of digital mind welfare, the simulation hypothesis is one reason to be supportive.

C. Testing the AGI Simulation Hypothesis

There are a few ways we could get weak evidence for whether or not the AGI simulation hypothesis is true:

  • The AGI sim hypothesis predicts short timelines. If you're reading this post fifty years later and AGI turned out much harder to achieve than we thought and it doesn't seem likely anytime soon, that's evidence against this hypothesis.
  • The AGI sim hypothesis predicts there's high uncertainty about how the AGI transition will go. If our simulator is running Monte Carlo simulations, they'd concentrate the runs where there's the most variance, since it's less worthwhile to run sims where the outcome is more obvious. It is literally true that Trump being President is evidence for the simulation hypothesis. The more undetermined you think the future is, the more this should shift you towards the simulation hypothesis.

D. Your Childhood Might Not Have Happened To You

If the simulator is compute constrained, it's wasteful to run your childhood, since it isn't as relevant to the AGI transition. Instead, they might just run one sim of the world when you were growing up, save that sim's state at some checkpoint, and spin up a larger number of sims from that checkpoint state. This is similar to how you can fork an LLM conversation at the tenth turn and the forked LLM has the memory of the earlier turns even if it didn't personally experience them.

This model of the world says it's very unlikely that the instance of you who's reading this actually experienced your childhood. Even fewer instances, or maybe none at all, would have experienced humanity's earlier history.

E. So What Should We Actually Do?

If we're in an AGI sim, your childhood might not have happened to you, but the present moment where you're reading this is a real moment the simulator is watching. The value of public conversations and the importance of digital minds are two of the AGI sim hypothesis' most robust implications.

If you're an altruist and you put any credence in the AGI sim hypothesis, I encourage you to think out loud about what the credences you put in the above EA Decision Tree imply about your priorities. In a world that’s being watched, reasoning in public might be one of the most valuable things you can do.

  1. ^

    The most explicit prior statement of this hypothesis I've found is here.

  2. ^

    There are many more reasons why simulation arguments might dampen future fanaticism.

  3. ^

     This is one version of the argument from Wei Dai’s Beyond Astronomical Waste.
